context_blurb:
Why do the planets circle the Sun instead of flying off into space? Johannes Kepler found the rules they follow, and Isaac Newton explained those rules with one law of gravity, a law later used to time a comet, find a planet and weigh the Earth.

Tycho Brahe, the last great astronomer to work without a telescope, logged Mars for nearly twenty years, and Kepler inherited his records. Kepler's best model of Mars still missed some sightings by eight arcminutes, roughly a quarter of the Moon's width. Tycho's own errors were only one or two arcminutes, far smaller than the gap, so the fault had to lie in the model, and Kepler threw it out. Those eight minutes, he wrote, would lead the way to the reform of all astronomy.

The shape that worked, published in 1609 in Astronomia Nova, was an ellipse, with the Sun off its centre at a focus, one of two points along the long axis. Kepler found it the hard way: an egg-shaped path missed by eight arcminutes in the other direction, and the truth lay between. The planets' ellipses are nearly round; drawn to scale, Mars's path looks almost like a circle.

Kepler's second law says the line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so Earth moves faster along its path when nearer the Sun. Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, so it crosses the northern winter stretch of its orbit a few days quicker than the summer stretch. The tilt makes the seasons but not this difference: in the south, winter is the longest season.

Newton asked whether the pull that drops an apple also holds the Moon, which lies about sixty Earth radii from Earth's centre; sixty times sixty is 3,600. The Moon's fall each second, bending it off a straight course, is about 3,600 times smaller than an apple's in its first second, so Earth's pull weakens with the square of the distance. Twice as far, a pull is a quarter as strong.

Kepler's third law says the farther out a planet lies, the longer its year. Saturn lies about nine and a half times as far out as Earth, yet takes nearly thirty years to go round. Saturn moves more slowly, because the Sun's pull out there is weaker, at about 9.7 kilometres a second, a third of Earth's speed. Newton showed why: so weak a pull can hold a planet on its curved path only at a slower speed.

Newton weighed Jupiter by how fast its moons circle it at their distances, since the stronger a planet's pull, the faster a moon must go round to stay in orbit. The four large moons Galileo found in 1610 gave Jupiter about a thousandth of the Sun's mass. A planet's own trip round the Sun reveals almost nothing of its mass: small asteroids sharing Jupiter's path take the same 12 years.

Newton's law says every mass pulls on every other, so Halley's comet feels the pull of Jupiter and Saturn as it passes them, which Halley had blamed for its uneven laps. Before its return, Alexis Clairaut, Joseph Lalande and Nicole-Reine Lepaute worked out that those two planets would delay it by 618 days. It rounded the Sun in March 1759, within about a month of their forecast, one of the first great tests of Newton's law.

In 1797 and 1798 Henry Cavendish hung a long rod from a thin wire, with little lead balls on its ends, and set a big lead ball beside each, so the wire's twist measured the big balls' sideways tug. A small ball's weight is Earth's pull on it, and a body's pull depends on its mass alone, whatever it is made of. So comparing the two pulls told Cavendish how many big balls' worth of mass Earth holds. He gave it as Earth's average density, about 5.5 times that of water and far above the crust's, evidence for a dense metal core.

Uranus, too, wandered from its predicted path, first running ahead and then lagging. Working from the drift alone, the Paris mathematician Urbain Le Verrier calculated that an unseen planet farther out was pulling on Uranus, and where it must be. On 23 September 1846 Johann Galle and Heinrich d'Arrest in Berlin found Neptune less than a degree from his spot. Some had doubted Newton's law so far from the Sun; instead it led Le Verrier to a new planet.
